title: Reading That MIT Report on AI as a High School Teacher
author: The Broken Copier
summary: Writing as a public high school teacher in Oregon rather than an elite-university insider, the author works through MIT's Ad Hoc Committee report on AI in teaching and learning, arguing it offers genuine value even to K-12 educators far removed from MIT's resources. The piece highlights the report's honest naming of harms beyond just cheating — fraying trust between students and teachers, increasing isolation, and challenges to community norms around rigor and collaborative problem solving — and praises its eight guiding principles (from 'be humble' to 'augmentation not automation') for pairing abstractions with concrete examples rather than settling for cliché. The author is especially struck by the report's refusal to collapse contradictions into simple answers, quoting its line that 'preserving what's most important will require deliberate change,' and by its extended, action-oriented treatment of concerns like inequitable access to advanced AI tools and data privacy, rather than merely naming them. The piece closes by extracting three takeaways for K-12 teachers: that consensus on AI policy is neither achievable nor necessary, that trust and community remain nonnegotiable regardless of any specific AI policy, and that ongoing conversation matters more than any single fixed rule.
points: Applying an elite university's institutional report to a 2,000-student Oregon public high school context tests whether MIT's AI recommendations generalize beyond resource-rich, selective institutions — the author explicitly interrogates rather than assumes that transferability.

The report's naming of 'increasing isolation' and 'fraying trust between students and teachers' as AI-driven harms, beyond the more commonly discussed cheating and skill-erosion concerns, broadens the frame of what AI accountability in education needs to address.

The line 'paradoxically, preserving what's most important will require deliberate change' is highlighted as a model for holding institutional continuity and necessary reform together, rather than treating them as opposed goals.

The author's three K-12 takeaways — that consensus isn't achievable or necessary, that trust and community are nonnegotiable independent of specific AI rules, and that ongoing classroom conversation matters more than fixed policy — translate an institutional report into a practical framework any individual teacher can apply.
quotes: I do struggle at times when the decisions of elite, quite-selective schools drive discourse in education-from Alpha School's personalized AI tutoring program to Harvard faculty's capping of A's to the University of Michigan's movement towards pass/fail grade reporting.

The eight principles that the committee offers as driving the report: Be humble; Be bold; Put humanity at the center; Lean into learning; Teach with intentionality; No one size fits alls; Augmentation not automation; and Think beyond the classroom and the campus.
We believe the circumstances call for a substantial reshaping of the student experience... Paradoxically, preserving what's most important will require deliberate change.

Today, members of the MIT community share information with AI systems that includes the most personal and sensitive aspects of their identity and experience, posing questions about their health, relationships, emotional lives, goals, aspirations, and anxieties.

[AI] is imposing new pressures on a community still working to restore the foundational habits and attitudes that residential education depends on: showing up, building trust, enthusiastically joining shared efforts, and living with an easy sense of mutual obligation.
Trust, connection and community continue to be nonnegotiable. Are you building trust in your classroom and context? Are you designing for connection amongst students and adults?
